newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Parachute failure blamed for Indonesia plane crash.
newsitem.headline: Parachute failure blamed for Indonesia plane crash.

text.p: Indonesian authorities said on Tuesday that a faulty parachute cord triggered the crash of a locally-made military plane last month, killing all six people on board.

In a detailed explanation that appeared aimed at reassuring potential foreign buyers of the craft, military officials said the twin-engined turbo-prop CN-235-220 military aircraft crashed as a result of a chain reaction started by a parachute cord snapping during a low-altitude test flight.

The press briefing, unusual for Indonesia's usually tight-lipped military, came only a few weeks before the country planned to display a similar maritime patrol aircraft and its latest home-grown N-250 commuter plane at the Paris Air Show.

"There was no sign of a fault in either the aircraft, the aircraft's systems or the test procedures used by the aircraft's crew," said Air Force Lieutenant-Colonel Syarkiputeh, head of the team that investigated the crash.

A senior defence department official said the unusual openness about the crash of the CN-235, jointly designed with CASA of Spain as a 44-seat passenger aircraft with both military and civilian models, was to protect Indonesia's reputation as it seeks foreign buyers of the aircraft, including the Royal Australian Air Force.
"We have had to be open because this is our national plane and we want to sell it overseas," said the official, who asked not to be named.

The military version of the CN-235, made by state-owned Industri Pesawat Terbang Nusantara (IPTN) and piloted by the country's most experienced test pilot, Erwin Danuwinata, crashed on May 22 at the Gorda military airfield near Serang in West Java.
IPTN, controlled by high-profile Research and Technology Minister Jusuf Habibie, has already released a video of the crash taken by a chase plane as well as a camera on the ground.
Syarkiputeh said the accident occurred during a High Altitude Parachute Extraction System (HAPES) test as the aircraft was flying at 1,100 feet with a four-tonne test load of sand.
He said the cord tying the two small extraction parachutes to the test load broke after being deployed.
"There was a mistake in use of the type of parachute strap," he said. A lower-stress cord, which looked the same as the stronger higher-stress cord, was mistakenly used, he added.

Syarkiputeh said that since the test was supervised by an employee from the U.S.-based extraction system maker, the American instructor, William Denton, who died in the crash must take responsibility for the choice of the wrong parachute cord.
He said that broken parachutes are not unusual and the standard procedure in such a case would be to push the load out or bring it back into the aircraft's cargo hold to restore balance.

However, he said that after the cord broke a clevis, or U-shaped piece of metal used for attaching the extraction system's tackle, then fell from the load bay ceiling onto the open rear ramp of the aircraft, blocking the load from being jettisoned.
The clevis wedged under the 4.88 metre (16 feet) long load and prevented it from being dropped. A 2.75 metre (9 feet) length of the broken parachute strap then blew back between the load and ramp.
"The shifting of the centre of balance of the aircraft caused it to become unstable and crash. The low altitude made it impossible for the pilot to take emergency action," Syarkiputeh said.
I Made Sadha, the department's director-general for material facilities and service, said the Indonesian armed forces would continue to use the aircraft.
"The incident does not lessen the pride and trust of the Indonesian armed forces in using the military version of the CN-235 aircraft," he told the news conference.
